tldr: Without external cameras or motion capture, and under poor on-board sensing where the ball is easily lost, combining a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) with a small amount of demonstration data allows a bipedal robot to achieve a 100% goal scoring success rate after only 30 minutes of real-world training.
hero_caption: The real-robot experimental setup. Without any external instrumentation like external cameras or motion capture, the NAOv6 robot autonomously learns to dribble a ball into a goal using only its own cameras and odometry.
overview:
Enabling robots to learn skills directly from trial and error in the physical world, just like humans, is a longstanding dream of robot reinforcement learning. Outside instrumented lab environments, however, state estimates from on-board sensors are noisy. When targets leave the field of view, the robot easily loses track of them. In bipedal soccer dribbling in particular, walking sway and close proximity to the ball frequently cause the ball to disappear from sight. These failures in state estimation corrupt both policy inputs and reward computation, posing a major challenge.

To solve this, the authors developed "RSSM-RLPD," a new method that places a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) on top of the robot's existing state estimator (UKF). Crucially, they built an "observation-gated" predictive model. It corrects the latent state using observations (posterior update) only when the ball is observed, and maintains the state through its own predictions (prior) when the ball is lost. Furthermore, by backpropagating both future prediction loss and critic (value function) gradients simultaneously, the model acquires the memory representations truly needed to complete the task.

In experiments on a physical NAOv6 robot, using only 50 demonstration episodes and 30 minutes of real-world interaction, the robot achieved a 100% goal success rate from multiple starting positions (compared to 0% for a memoryless baseline). Simulation comparisons also showed superior sample efficiency that cannot be achieved simply by adding a recurrent neural network (GRU). This proves that an observation-gated predictive memory is a powerful tool for real-world reinforcement learning under imperfect state estimation.
contributions: Demonstrated that a bipedal robot can learn dribbling skills directly on physical hardware using only imperfect on-board state estimates, without relying on any external instrumentation.

Proposed an observation-gated RSSM that switches between updating the latent state (posterior) and predicting it (prior) based on ball visibility, extracting robust state representations from imperfect estimates.
Constructed a representation learning framework that combines future observation and interaction prediction losses with critic TD error gradients to efficiently form task-relevant memory.

Achieved a 100% goal success rate in validation tests including unseen starting positions after only 30 minutes of real-robot interaction and 50 demonstrations, significantly outperforming existing baselines.

sections.heading: Why is real-world learning so hard? The trap of partial observability and state estimation
sections.summary: While reinforcement learning in real-world environments is advancing rapidly, most setups rely on external cameras or benign observations. This section introduces the core challenges faced when learning purely from imperfect on-board sensors: ball loss and state estimation collapse.
sections.details:
Applying reinforcement learning to robots has seen remarkable progress recently. Quadruped locomotion and robotic arm manipulation can increasingly be mastered in hours or even minutes. However, many of these success stories rely on overhead cameras, motion capture systems, or environments where the state is almost fully observable.

In real-world settings without such special equipment, robots must estimate the world state relying solely on their own on-board cameras and sensors. Yet, due to heavy body sway during walking and blind spots when moving close to the ball, the target object (the ball) frequently leaves the field of view. Estimates from an on-board UKF (unscented Kalman filter, which estimates nonlinear states) quickly lose reliability once the target is lost, continuing to produce incorrect values. This corrupts not only the policy input, but also the reward signals guiding learning.

This study tackles a contact-rich, highly partially observable bipedal soccer task. Building on RLPD (an efficient real-robot RL method that mixes online trials with offline demonstrations during replay), the authors propose an approach that layers an RSSM (recurrent state-space model) over the UKF to learn a latent belief resilient to interrupted observations.

captions.F1: The NAOv6 robot and field used as the stage for real-world experiments. In this demanding environment without external sensors, the robot learns to dribble and score using only its own cameras and imperfect state estimates.

sections.heading: Where do existing methods fall short? The lineage of world models and memory
sections.summary: This section reviews sample-efficient real-robot RL, memory structures for solving POMDPs (partially observable Markov decision processes), and prior work in robot soccer. It clarifies the paper's unique approach to leveraging world model predictive capabilities under intermittent real-world observations.
sections.details:
Related work falls into three main areas:

### Sample-Efficient Real-Robot RL
In real-robot reinforcement learning, reducing the number of trials is critical. Methods like RLPD and SERL build on efficient actor-critic algorithms like SAC and REDQ, sampling a small number of human demonstrations alongside online experience from replay buffers. Works like DayDreamer learn a world model directly on hardware to optimize policies in imagination. However, contact-rich tasks where ball contact and intermittent visual loss occur simultaneously remain extremely challenging for these existing approaches.

### Memory and Predictive Representations
In POMDP environments where the state is not fully visible, recurrent neural networks (like GRUs and LSTMs) that summarize history have served as standard baselines. Going a step further, approaches like DVRL and SLAC train generative models and latent dynamics concurrently to assist memory. This study adopts the RSSM structure used in systems like Dreamer, but differs by cleanly decoupling the robot's own motion context from intermittent ball observations, using an update mechanism that only applies corrections when observations are actually present.

### Reinforcement Learning in Robot Soccer
Many prior studies train policies in simulation and transfer them using Sim-to-Real to achieve agile soccer motions. Other efforts combine classical localization modules with learned control. This work leverages an existing modular estimator, corrects its imperfect estimates using predictive memory, and aims to directly learn goal-scoring skills from minimal real-robot experience.

sections.heading: System and task setup: Self-contained on-board sensing and rewards
sections.summary: The soccer task on the NAOv6 is formulated as a POMDP, detailing inputs, outputs, and reward design. In particular, observation freshness gating prevents false rewards from imperfect state estimates, which is key to stabilizing real-robot learning.
sections.details:
### Task Formulation and Robot Platform
The task is to dribble a ball on the field and score a goal. A bipedal humanoid NAOv6 is used, with computation running on an external workstation (equipped with an RTX 5090) connected via Wi-Fi. No external instrumentation is used; only data received and estimated by the robot is transmitted to the workstation.

### Observation and Action Design
A 12-dimensional observation vector $\boldsymbol{o}_t$ is formed using the on-board UKF and ball tracker. It includes the ball position and velocity in robot coordinates, and the relative pose between the robot and the goal. When the ball is not visible, position is replaced with sentinel values, velocity is set to zero, and a confidence metric $\rho_t = \exp[-\tau_t / 0.5\,\text{s}]$ based on time elapsed $\tau_t$ since the last observation is provided to the policy. The action space is 3-dimensional, specifying forward velocity, lateral velocity, and yaw rotational velocity. These are sent to the walking controller at a 30 Hz control frequency after smoothing and safety filtering.

### Reward Design to Prevent False Rewards
Rewards comprise ball approach ($r_t^{\text{app}}$), ball progress toward the goal ($r_t^{\text{goal}}$), facing the ball ($r_t^{\text{bear}}$), and more. A crucial design detail is that the forward progress reward is only given when the ball has been continuously observed recently ($\chi_t=1$). This blocks false positive rewards if the UKF outputs incorrect estimates while the ball is lost. Conversely, penalties accumulate if the ball remains lost for an extended period.

sections.heading: Proposed method 'RSSM-RLPD': A smart memory model switching predictions on observation
sections.summary: This section explains RSSM-RLPD, the core technique of this paper. Key features include an observation-gated belief that corrects with the posterior when the ball is visible and maintains self-predictions with the prior when it is not, along with joint representation learning using prediction losses and critic gradients.
sections.details:
This method docks an observation-gated recurrent state-space model (RSSM) into RLPD (a sample-efficient actor-critic method that balances demonstrations and online trials equally).

### Observation-Gated Latent Belief
The RSSM latent state consists of a 128-dimensional deterministic state $\boldsymbol{h}_t$ updated by a GRU, and a 16-dimensional stochastic state $\boldsymbol{z}_t$. The key innovation is switching the latent state update depending on whether the ball is observed:
- **When the ball is observed**: The state is updated (corrected) via a posterior head $q_\theta(\boldsymbol{z}_t \mid \boldsymbol{h}_t, \boldsymbol{o}_t^{\text{ball}})$ that takes the ball observation $\boldsymbol{o}_t^{\text{ball}}$ as input.
- **When the ball is not observed**: The state directly uses a prior head $p_\theta(\boldsymbol{z}_t \mid \boldsymbol{h}_t)$ based only on the robot's own motion context.
As a result, the state resets to accurate values while the ball is visible, and when hidden by the feet or blind spots, the robot continues to predict the ball's location in its mind based on its walking actions.

### Hybrid Learning with Prediction Losses and Critic Gradients
This latent representation is guided not just by predicting the next observation, but by several loss functions:
- **Reconstruction and Prediction Losses**: Decoders predict relative ball position, reward, episode termination flags, and ball contact from replay data. A multi-step prediction loss predicting ball position 1 to 40 steps into the future is also included.
- **Gradients from the Critic**: Gradients from the policy learning critic flow directly into the RSSM. This adapts the predictive model to prioritize retaining information critical for scoring goals, rather than just physical prediction.

### Replay Masking Augmentation
During training, segments (6 to 36 steps) of trajectory data drawn from the replay buffer are intentionally masked to simulate ball loss. Because the underlying data is complete, this offline training reinforces the model's ability to correctly recover state even after losing sight of the ball.

sections.heading: Experimental results: 100% success after 30 minutes on hardware, verified in simulation
sections.summary: The method was evaluated on both the physical NAO and in simulation. On hardware, 30 minutes of training enabled scoring from all three starting positions, achieving a 100% success rate in validation tests. Simulation confirmed superior sample efficiency over a standard GRU.
sections.details:
### Real-Robot Training and Evaluation
In real-robot experiments, the ball was placed at three starting positions near the penalty area (center, left, right). The training budget was just 7,000 action steps (about 30 minutes of physical operating time).

The results were striking. The proposed RSSM-RLPD scored its first goal only 10 minutes into training and scored 9 goals across the session. Meanwhile, GRU-RLPD, a standard recurrent baseline, took 20 minutes to its first goal and reached only 4 goals total. Memoryless FF-RLPD (feed-forward) and behavior cloning (BC) failed to score even once within the training budget.

Next, a validation test (16-minute time limit) was run from 5 positions: the 3 training positions plus 2 unseen positions. With a 4-minute limit per trial, RSSM-RLPD cleared all 5 positions in under 10 minutes, reaching a **100% success rate**. GRU-RLPD achieved 80% (taking 16 minutes), FF-RLPD scored only 1 goal (counted as 0% success), and BC scored 0 goals.

### Detailed Simulation Verification
In simulation, each method was trained across 5 random seeds for 100k steps. RSSM-RLPD consistently led GRU-RLPD, showing a significant 12.45-point lead in AUC (area under the curve from 0 to 60k steps), a measure of sample efficiency. Diagnostic analysis (Table V) showed that RSSM-RLPD had the highest ball contact rate and an extremely low rate of timeouts from losing the ball for 10 seconds. This demonstrates that the observation-gated model accurately remembers where the ball is.

sections.heading: Limitations and future work: Fine foot control and reliance on demonstrations
sections.summary: While demonstrating remarkable physical performance, challenges remain, such as reliance on fixed demonstrations and coarse commands to the walking controller. End-to-end integration with the state estimator and finer foot contact control are directions for future work.
sections.details:
The authors highlight three main limitations and future directions:

- **Reliance on Demonstration Data**: The method uses a fixed set of 50 demonstration episodes collected on the real robot. Sensitivity analyses on demonstration quality and quantity, as well as incorporating human interventions during training, remain to be explored.
- **Coupling with Estimator Errors**: Because the model is built on top of the existing UKF, it is impacted when the UKF produces extreme estimation errors. Training the estimator and recurrent memory end-to-end could yield greater robustness.
- **Control Abstraction Level**: The policy outputs high-level velocity commands (forward, lateral, yaw) for the whole body, leaving precise foot placement and ball contact to the low-level walking controller. Achieving more delicate dribbling and varied soccer skills will require direct foot-level contact control supported by more advanced state estimation.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Robots can learn autonomously even with imperfect sensors
sections.summary: This study proves that combining an observation-gated RSSM with demonstration-augmented RLPD makes real-world reinforcement learning feasible even with poor on-board sensing. It has the potential to set a new standard for physical learning under partial observability.
sections.details:
This paper introduced RSSM-RLPD, which learns a contact-rich soccer task without external instrumentation, relying only on imperfect on-board state estimates.

By correcting latent state only when the ball is observed, maintaining memory through prediction when it is lost, and combining prediction losses with critic gradients, the robot achieved a 100% goal success rate in just 30 minutes of real-world interaction. Simulation studies also confirmed sample efficiency and robustness that cannot be matched by simply adding standard recurrent networks like GRUs.

These results provide strong optimism that robots can acquire sophisticated motor skills outside the lab in noisy real-world environments, guided solely by their own sensors and physical experience.

takeaways: On physical robots lacking external instrumentation, an observation-gated predictive model built to handle interrupted state estimates works exceptionally well.
Training recurrent state-space model (RSSM) representations with both future prediction losses and critic value gradients builds memory directly aligned with task success.
Using replay masking augmentation to intentionally obscure observations in offline data significantly boosts the ability to infer states when targets are lost on hardware.
Combining a small number of high-quality demonstrations with suitable predictive representation learning allows bipedal contact-rich policies to converge in roughly 30 minutes of physical trials.
limitations: Relies on a fixed set of 50 demonstration episodes, and sensitivity or robustness to reduced demonstration quality or quantity has not been fully verified.
Because the learned model sits on top of an existing UKF state estimator, it cannot easily recover from catastrophic upstream failures such as complete localization loss.
The policy outputs coarse velocity commands, leaving the fine-grained contact dynamics of foot placement and kicking unmanaged by direct control.
